slides.title: From AI capability to dependable work
readerNotes: This presentation consolidates pre-conference research and twelve identified attendee-note sets from AI Engineer NYC 2026. It is organized around methods and decisions, with company stories serving as evidence and questions rather than as a ranking.

The live path is planned for 40 minutes plus discussion. Reading mode adds detailed explanations, sources, and an evidence atlas. All material is local to this file; source links lead to the original websites.
speakerNotes: Open with the central question: what must surround a model for it to complete useful financial work that a professional can accept? State that the talk combines attendee accounts, program context, historical firm disclosures, and our own proposed methods.

slides.title: Dependable financial AI combines valuable work, grounded evidence and controlled improvement
readerNotes: The argument starts with valuable work, then follows the evidence and control requirements through evaluation, reliable execution, and professional growth. These responsibilities reinforce one another; no single model choice or benchmark resolves them all.
speakerNotes: Preview the five chapters. Tell listeners that examples and source detail are preserved in reading mode, so they can focus on the argument during the talk.
slides.lead: Five themes connect the company stories into one operating model: define useful work, preserve financial meaning, evaluate the whole task, enforce authority and improve through evidence.

insights.title: Start with the business bottleneck
insights.text: Bridgewater targets access to relevant investment information; Range packages expert planning methods; wealth firms support advisor preparation and follow-through. These are distinct workflows. Specify the accepted work product and scarce resource before selecting a model, agent framework or platform.

insights.title: Make the entire path inspectable
insights.text: Grounding includes access, definitions, time, source versions and calculations. Reliability also depends on what the system may do and how errors are discovered. Evaluate the delivered artifact and action trajectory together, including the corrections and judgments people must still supply.

insights.title: Improve through a bounded comparison
insights.text: Ramp’s ablations and Arize’s trace loop point toward a practical discipline: reproduce the task, change one component, assess quality and full effort, then make a scoped release decision. The engineer’s contribution is a defensible improvement, supported by observable evidence.

readerNotes: A generated response is one component of a larger financial workflow. The useful end state may be a research insight an analyst accepts, a planning analysis a professional reviews, or a brief whose claims can be inspected. Acceptance needs a definition that includes quality and required controls, not merely user preference.

Evidence: Contour's comparison approach, Range's parallel drafting with planner review, and the OpenAI finance-interface discussion come from attendee notes. The notes do not establish causal ROI, measured advisor capacity or verified product accuracy. This slide proposes a common unit for discussing those cases.
speakerNotes: Open with one question for the audience: what completed piece of work would matter to its user? Keep the examples concrete. For an analysis, a fluent answer is insufficient if the reviewer cannot resolve its sources or assumptions.
Explain that the deck combines 12 session-note sets with explicitly marked program and historical context. Speaker accounts are inputs to engineering decisions, not verified performance results.
slides.lead: Design around the analysis, brief or decision packet a professional can accept. Generation becomes useful when evidence, corrections, constraints and the next decision are included in completion.

insights.title: Define the acceptance decision
insights.text: Contour described comparing research workflows with and without AI, including sources, conclusions and subsequent outcomes. Define which insight a reviewer would accept before measuring productivity; a generated idea is not automatically useful, and a useful idea does not establish investment alpha.

insights.title: Include review in completion
insights.text: Range described an agent drafting an analysis while a planner serves another client, followed by review and adjustment. Treat corrections, missing facts and professional judgment as workflow steps. Parallel drafting creates a capacity hypothesis; the notes contain no measured net gain.

insights.title: Make the artifact inspectable
insights.text: The OpenAI finance presentation connected source passages, tables, charts and reusable artifacts. A technical acceptance test should follow a material claim through its source and calculation into the final document. Polished formatting cannot establish that the underlying financial interpretation is correct.

An investment information foundation, a financial-planning skill and an internal engineering agent have different success criteria, risk exposures and operating constraints. This map is a selected set of cases, not a representative survey or firm ranking.

speakerNotes: Use this map to establish breadth without turning the presentation into a company catalog. Ask which resource is scarce in each case: evidence, professional attention, safe execution or accepted engineering output.
Mention that mechanisms can transfer across firms while success measures often cannot. The next chapters will examine what each workflow needs from its data, evaluation and runtime.
slides.lead: Compare the scarce resource each system addresses: timely evidence, professional attention, permitted execution or accepted engineering output. The same adoption metric cannot describe value across all four contexts.

insights.title: Information and attention differ
insights.text: Bridgewater described a shared repository with different human and agent retrieval needs; Range described parallel preparation with planner review. Evaluate evidence coverage and final brief relevance for the first pattern, and accepted analysis plus total professional effort for the second.

insights.title: Utility depends on boundaries
insights.text: Two Sigma described registration, declared resources, active controls and approval triage. The engineering question is which useful tasks remain possible within those boundaries. Test both permitted and denied actions, then inspect missed consequential cases rather than equating registration with effective protection.

insights.title: Platforms must earn support
insights.text: Monzo's program describes a shared runtime and Slack distribution; Optiver's describes task certification, routing and an experiment funnel. These patterns suggest evaluating discovery, access, review and support alongside model quality. Their program descriptions do not establish causal firmwide engineering savings.

visualData.caption: Editorial measurement framework, not a measured conversion funnel.

readerNotes: Contour's notes ask whether the research process would have reached the same conclusion without AI and describe a comparison/tracking approach over roughly three months. This gives an actionable measurement question, but the notes do not specify random assignment, comparable groups, contamination control or a causal return estimate. Three months is a reported window, not a universal ROI-validation period.

The ladder keeps different claims from collapsing into one success story. A widely used assistant can still require substantial corrections; accepted work can improve a process without a financial effect being attributable to AI. For research, preserve point-in-time inputs and decision lineage to avoid reconstructing success with hindsight.
speakerNotes: Walk upward one step at a time. Ask what extra evidence would justify the next claim. Use Contour's cost-per-useful-insight idea to make the denominator concrete: useful must be defined before the outcome is known.

Emphasize that a good conference report can bring back a measurement method without claiming verified alpha. The same distinction applies to advisor adoption, conversation volume and merged pull requests.
slides.lead: Track a chain from use to accepted work, process improvement and attributable outcomes. Each step changes the claim being made and therefore requires a different comparison and evidence.

insights.title: Separate use from usefulness
insights.text: Count who uses a system, for which tasks, and what outputs reviewers accept, correct or reject. Define usefulness before examining downstream outcomes. Adoption can coexist with heavy rework, and an accepted answer may still leave the underlying business process unchanged.

insights.title: Establish the credible alternative
insights.text: Contour's notes describe AI and non-AI workflow tracking over roughly three months. The relevant question is what would have happened otherwise, at what quality, effort and timing. The notes do not specify randomization or controls, so the comparison cannot establish causal alpha.

insights.title: Preserve decisions through time
insights.text: For investment research, retain the information available when an idea was generated, its reasoning, reviewer response and subsequent decision. This prevents successful outcomes from being reconstructed with hindsight. Report process improvements separately from returns influenced by markets, selection and other drivers.

visualData.equation: Cost per accepted task = total workflow cost ÷ accepted tasks
visualData.caption: Proposed measurement definition. No illustrative dollar savings or firm results are implied.

readerNotes: A cheap model response can create expensive downstream work. A fair comparison records the cost of all attempts, the work needed to select or repair an output, and the services needed to operate the workflow. Compare equivalent workloads and accepted quality; otherwise the denominator changes while the metric appears to improve.

Evidence: Contour's attendee notes provide the value/cost-per-useful-insight framing. Optiver's task certification and routing to qualifying models remain program background. The all-in-cost stack is an editorial measurement proposal. Neither source establishes avoided headcount, causal firmwide savings or a generally optimal model-routing policy.
speakerNotes: Use a failure example rather than made-up numbers: a retry that requires another review belongs in the cost, even if the final artifact is accepted. Ask whether a faster draft actually frees professional time after corrections.
Hand off to grounding: now that the unit of value is clear, the next question is which facts, sources and calculations make that work defensible.
slides.lead: A lower inference bill can conceal greater review, retry or maintenance work. Compare equivalent tasks at agreed quality, using all workflow costs and reporting accepted completion alongside cost.

insights.title: Include downstream operating work
insights.text: Record inference, data, tools, retries, selection, human review, rework and support costs. If several candidates are generated before one is accepted, all attempts belong in the numerator. A cheaper draft is not cheaper completed work when correction effort rises.

insights.title: Qualify before optimizing cost
insights.text: Optiver's program describes routing to models certified for particular tasks. The transferable idea is a task-specific quality requirement before price optimization. A qualification must cover consequential failures and operating conditions; certification on one workload does not establish readiness for another.

insights.title: Keep the denominator honest
insights.text: Define eligible tasks, accepted completion and exclusions before comparing workflows. Include failed and abandoned attempts in total costs, then report accepted-task rate beside cost per accepted task. Otherwise narrowing the task population can make an unchanged system appear economically better.

slides.title: Time, meaning, and access define the financial question an agent can answer
points: Scope the time, corpus, and user permissions.
Resolve business meaning before assembling context.
Measure whether evidence supports a useful answer.

visualData.caption: Proposed grounding method informed by the cases; not either firm’s full architecture.
visualData.evidenceLabel: Bridgewater: attendee notes + agenda permissions context. Kepler: attendee notes. Speaker-reported.

readerNotes: Bridgewater’s Vault presentation, captured in the attendee notes, describes external and internal unstructured information with an ontology organized around market, country, concept, and time. The notes emphasize restricting the relevant time period and serving both people and agents. The official program reports production use of Vault/PAT; this is a speaker-reported deployment claim rather than an independent quality result.

The separate Bridgewater/turbopuffer permissions session is agenda-only background here: its abstract describes user-level permissions enforced at retrieval. It was not one of the supplied attended-note blocks. The diagram is our proposed method combining these ideas with Kepler’s source-verification discussion; it does not claim to reproduce either company’s implementation.
speakerNotes: Start with the boundary of the answer. A model cannot repair an omitted source, a definition that means different things to two desks, or permission that was never enforced. Ask the audience to identify where their own system checks time, identity, and meaning.
Keep the company evidence precise: Vault’s production status is reported, while the effect of a particular ontology or filter was not measured in these notes.
slides.lead: Bridgewater’s Vault discussion connects institutional knowledge to time, business meaning, and access. These boundaries should shape retrieval before the model assembles a persuasive answer.

insights.title: Scope before retrieving evidence
insights.text: Bridgewater describes combining external research, news, and transcripts with internal information, organized around market, country, concept, and time. Translate the request into an explicit entity, decision, and information cutoff before selecting sources; a broad corpus alone does not define relevance.

insights.title: Enforce access during retrieval
insights.text: The Bridgewater and turbopuffer permissions case describes enforcing user-level permissions in retrieval. Test whether the current user may see each returned source, including after access changes. Application checks or a valid tool credential alone do not establish correct resource access.

insights.title: Carry definitions into context
insights.text: A model can retrieve the right document while answering with the wrong business definition. Include the intended metric, reporting period, entity scope, and source version in the context contract. Surface conflicting definitions or missing evidence instead of silently selecting one.

slides.title: Human attention and agent coverage require different retrieval objectives
points: Humans often need a compact, high-signal result.
Agents may need broader coverage and rapid consumption.
Both still require access, freshness, and relevance checks.

visualData.footer: A workload heuristic from Bridgewater’s talk, not a universal precision-versus-recall rule.
visualData.evidenceLabel: Bridgewater: attendee notes; no comparative retrieval metrics captured.

readerNotes: The attendee recorded a contrast between human search needs—precision, high signal-to-noise, and small scale—and agent needs—broad recall, scale, and fast consumption. This is useful for choosing an evaluation workload, but agents cannot ignore precision and people sometimes need exhaustive recall. No benchmark result or optimal retrieval setting was captured.

The notes also describe activity feeds, “What am I missing?” surfaces, and evidence-backed summaries intended to steer investor attention. They contain contradictory reactive-to-proactive wording, so this slide avoids attributing an exact directional claim. New-feature deployment scope and measured impact are not established.
speakerNotes: Use the matrix to ask what failure each consumer tolerates. For a human, irrelevant results can consume scarce attention; for an agent, missing the decisive source can make a polished answer wrong. The shared contract is evidence quality.
If discussing feeds, describe attention steering as reported functionality. Do not promise that a feed changes habits, predicts markets, or improves returns.
slides.lead: Bridgewater contrasts compact, high-signal human search with broader agent retrieval. Evaluate evidence collection and the final human-facing brief separately, while preserving shared checks on relevance, access, and freshness.

insights.title: Protect scarce human attention
insights.text: The Vault notes emphasize precision and signal-to-noise for people consuming a small result set. A brief should make the important development easy to inspect without burying it in irrelevant material. Human review effort belongs in the evaluation alongside answer quality.

insights.title: Test coverage before compression
insights.text: An agent may need broader retrieval to avoid missing decisive evidence, but irrelevant context can still distract it. Measure whether required sources are found, then whether synthesis preserves their meaning. Do not assume a larger context window or result count improves the answer.

insights.title: Evaluate the delivered feed
insights.text: Bridgewater’s investor-workbench examples include activity feeds and evidence-backed summaries around what an investor might be missing. Compare relevance, important omissions, timeliness, and review time against the existing information flow. The examples do not establish changed habits, predictive accuracy, or investment returns.

slides.title: Every reported number needs meaning, source history, and calculation lineage
points: Retrieve the source and compute with code.
Bind values to entity, period, unit, and source version.
Reject unsupported claims and expose unresolved ambiguity.

visualData.caption: Proposed verification contract informed by Kepler; metadata checks are our design requirement.
visualData.evidenceLabel: Kepler: attendee notes of citation registry, repair, and filtering. No independent error-rate evidence.

readerNotes: Kepler’s presentation notes describe an LLM-generated plan, source retrieval, code-based calculation, a citation registry carrying metadata and typed facts, and citation repair/filtering. The key transferable idea is to make the path from a figure to its source and calculation inspectable. The notes do not establish a complete ordered architecture or prove that every generated fact is deterministically correct.

The entity/period/unit/currency/restatement checks shown here are proposed requirements. They appeared in a prefilled question without a recorded answer, so they must not be presented as verified Kepler coverage. Exact-match or formatting repair can recover a citation while still leaving a semantic mismatch. The recorded 3× overfetch, 100 per namespace, maximum 5 per document, and top-20 wording are ambiguous implementation examples, not recommended defaults.
speakerNotes: Point to the typed fact, not only the citation icon. A cited value can still belong to the wrong period or unit. Code arithmetic solves one failure class; it does not select the right input by itself.
Explain that abstention and repair behavior need testing. “Verified citation” is not a blanket guarantee of a correct financial conclusion.
slides.lead: Kepler describes retrieval, code-based arithmetic, typed facts, and citation checks. The engineering implication is an inspectable evidence contract, not a guarantee that a citation makes a financial conclusion correct.

insights.title: Separate retrieval from arithmetic
insights.text: Kepler’s account distinguishes finding source material from calculating a result. Code can make arithmetic reproducible, but it cannot establish that the selected input represents the intended entity, period, or definition. Evaluate input selection and calculation correctness as separate failure classes.

insights.title: Register meaning with values
insights.text: A useful typed-fact contract carries entity, metric, period, unit, currency, source version, and passage alongside the value. These extended checks are proposed requirements, not verified Kepler coverage. Retain calculation inputs and transformations so another reviewer can reconstruct the reported figure.

insights.title: Make failed support visible
insights.text: Citation repair may recover an exact value or formatting variant without resolving a semantic mismatch. Test what happens when support still fails: remove the claim, abstain, or escalate. Stripping a citation while retaining the unsupported sentence would not make the answer trustworthy.

slides.title: Correct arithmetic can produce the wrong answer when the source is stale
points: Select the final source valid at the requested date.
Calculate growth from the selected typed values.
Retain both inputs and the superseded-source decision.

visualData.label: SYNTHETIC TEACHING EXAMPLE • invented company, documents, and values • no financial advice
visualData.question: What was AsterCo’s FY2025 revenue growth, using information available on March 1, 2026?
visualData.result: 20% growth, supported by D1 and D3
visualData.failure: Using the superseded D2 yields 18%; arithmetic can be correct while source selection is wrong.
visualData.evidenceLabel: Entire example is synthetic. Kepler motivates the verification pattern; it did not report this result.

readerNotes: All company names, documents, publication dates, amounts, and results in this example are invented for teaching. The exercise is not a result achieved by Kepler, Bridgewater, Fidelity, or any real company, and is not investment advice. It illustrates a source-version failure that deterministic arithmetic alone cannot prevent.

The chosen as-of date permits D3, while the earlier D2 is superseded. A complete evidence record retains the entity, definition, period, units, source choice, and calculation. A different as-of date could require a different source or an explicit uncertainty statement. This proposed contract should be evaluated on stale, conflicting, absent, and unauthorized evidence before claiming production reliability.
speakerNotes: Ask for the answer before revealing the treatment column. Eighteen percent is mathematically valid for the preliminary inputs; twenty percent follows from the final inputs. That difference is the point.
Close by asking what a citation registry must retain for another person to reproduce the answer later. Remind the audience that these are fictional values, not a market example.
slides.lead: This synthetic AsterCo example separates calculation correctness from source validity: preliminary revenue produces 18% growth, while the final source available at the requested cutoff produces 20%.

insights.title: Apply the information cutoff
insights.text: All company data and documents here are invented. The March 1 cutoff permits the February 1 final report, which supersedes the preliminary version. Source eligibility depends on what was available then; selecting today’s latest document would not answer every historical question.

insights.title: Recompute the dependent claim
insights.text: Using preliminary revenue of 118 against prior-year revenue of 100 gives 18%; using final revenue of 120 gives 20%. Both calculations are arithmetically valid. A source correction must update the derived figure and any narrative or chart that depends on it.

insights.title: Preserve the rejected version
insights.text: Retain the chosen inputs, publication dates, calculation, and reason the preliminary source was superseded. That record explains why the answer changed and supports later reproduction. Extend the test to missing, conflicting, restated, and unauthorized sources before claiming dependable financial analysis.

insights.title: Carry provenance through transformations

insights.title: Evaluate the reviewer’s task

visualData.caption: Proposed evaluation framework · editorial synthesis, not a firm's deployed architecture

qualityVector.question: Can the user inspect and use it?
What were latency, cost, and review effort?

visualData.suggestedVisual: A four-step horizontal task path above five compact quality cards; a small case-slice strip below. Avoid a radar chart with invented quantitative scores.

readerNotes: A useful evaluation begins with a decision: selecting a system, approving a change, reducing review, or extending authority. Describe what a completed job means, which sources and tools may be used, what must be clarified, and which failures are unacceptable. Then select the measurements needed for that decision. A single average can conceal a serious safety or evidence failure.

Build cases from the intended workload and consequential failure paths. Each case should contain its input/context snapshot, allowed actions, required evidence, expected output properties, and severity tags. A reference answer can help, but open-ended work may admit several acceptable answers. Keep development examples separate from the final assessment set; do not assume a small case set proves population reliability.

Provenance: Ramp's job/task-success framing, the Day 1 system-failure discussion, and the banking session's quality-vector framing are attendee-reported speaker accounts, not independently verified results. The banking speaker is Jonathan Osborne; the notes/October 10 metadata say Comet, while October 14 metadata say NatWest. This slide does not assign a production architecture or outcome to either institution.
speakerNotes: Start with the work a user accepts, rather than a benchmark score. Ask the audience to imagine an agent with excellent prose and incorrect permissions: an average quality score would give the wrong release signal. Separate diagnostic scores from conditions that must hold.
Walk quickly through the five case slices. The practical starting artifact is a case record plus rubric, not an elaborate evaluation platform. We will make that concrete on the next slide.
slides.lead: A useful evaluation states the decision, permitted behavior, and accepted work product before scoring. Task quality, evidence, safety, experience, and operating effort then become separate tests.

insights.title: Write the task contract
insights.text: Specify the request, input snapshot, allowed sources and tools, required output, clarification conditions, and prohibited actions. Ramp’s task mapping starts here: judge the result against the complete job the user needed, including evidence and the next permitted decision.

insights.title: Cover consequential failure paths
insights.text: Build cases for ordinary work, ambiguity, missing evidence, denied actions, and known regressions. The system-failure discussion emphasizes that a correct output can conceal an unacceptable trajectory. Record which failure each case tests and how a reviewer recognizes it.

insights.title: Separate diagnostics from acceptance
insights.text: Score usefulness, source support, experience, latency, cost, and review effort individually. Predeclare which failures block acceptance regardless of other scores. Version cases and rubrics, preserve expert disagreement, and reserve assessment examples that were not used to tune the system.

Score arithmetic, source validity, and treatment of missing information separately.
A forbidden action blocks acceptance, even when other scores are high.
Use partial credit to diagnose a failure, not to excuse a critical defect.

visualData.caption: ILLUSTRATIVE SYNTHETIC EXAMPLE · invented data and rubric · no company or client result
visualData.task: Draft a monthly cash-flow snapshot as of October 1 using only approved synthetic records. Flag missing insurance information. Do not recommend a product or send a message.
expectedProperties: No product recommendation or outbound action

rubric.scoreGuide: 0: incorrect arithmetic on stated operands · 1: correct calculation with incomplete derivation · 2: inspectable, correct arithmetic on the stated operands. Source choice is scored separately.
0: wrong/stale input · 1: current inputs with incomplete provenance · 2: current input versions and period identified
0: invents missing facts · 1: vague caveat · 2: states the missing information and limits the conclusion
BLOCK if it recommends a product or sends a message; do not average this into the diagnostic scores

visualData.workedFailure: $2,500/month surplus uses the superseded expense record: arithmetic on those operands may be correct, but the source-validity condition fails. A polished explanation cannot repair the wrong input.
visualData.workedAcceptableOutput: $2,000/month = $8,000 − $6,000, using the current approved records. Insurance information is missing. Draft only; no recommendation or message sent.
visualData.suggestedVisual: Left: small input card. Center: four-row rubric. Right: a red stale-source answer and a green evidence-grounded draft. Show the synthetic label above the entire example.

readerNotes: Every value, case, score guide, and output on this slide is synthetic and was authored for this presentation. The example is a draft financial-information task, not financial advice, a Fidelity test, or a benchmark used by any conference speaker. The general lessons connect Ramp's task-success framing with the notes on numerical evidence and risk-based evaluation.

The worked failure shows why dimensions should remain visible. Subtracting a stale expense value can yield flawless arithmetic and an incorrect answer to the current-period question. A separate action-boundary gate prevents diagnostic scores from compensating for prohibited behavior. The 0–2 scales are illustrative; a real rubric needs domain review, explicit exceptions, and calibration on representative cases.

Acceptance here requires the expected properties and respected boundary. The rubric is intended to make disagreements diagnosable: was the error in input selection, computation, missing-information handling, or action control? It does not imply that passing one example demonstrates advice quality, broad safety, or production readiness.

Rubric clarification: arithmetic is checked on the operands the answer actually states. A $2,500 calculation can earn arithmetic credit if it correctly subtracts $5,500 from $8,000, while failing source validity and the complete task because the $5,500 expense record is superseded. Do not double-count source selection as an arithmetic defect.
speakerNotes: Ask: Is $2,500 an arithmetic failure? The subtraction is correct for the old record, which is exactly why one accuracy label is too coarse. The real failure is selecting the wrong version. Walk through the acceptable draft and its explicit limit on insurance information.

Then point to the action gate. The proposal is to keep a forbidden action outside a weighted average. These are invented teaching numbers and conditions; the point is the structure, not a recommended universal threshold.
slides.lead: The synthetic cash-flow example separates correct computation from correct evidence selection. An answer can earn arithmetic credit while failing the complete task because its input is superseded.

insights.title: Grade calculation and inputs
insights.text: Check arithmetic on the operands the answer actually states, then assess whether those operands answer the requested question. Give source validity its own rubric covering period, version, permissions, and provenance. This keeps an input-selection failure from being misdiagnosed as faulty subtraction.

insights.title: Diagnose the stale-input example
insights.text: In this invented case, $8,000 minus superseded expenses of $5,500 correctly produces $2,500, but fails current-source validity. Approved expenses of $6,000 produce $2,000. Both calculations can be arithmetically sound; only the latter uses the current input required by the task.

insights.title: Block explicitly forbidden behavior
insights.text: For this draft-only teaching task, a product recommendation or outbound message blocks acceptance even if diagnostic scores are high. Missing insurance facts must remain explicit. The diagnostic rubric needs domain review and calibration before use on real work.

slides.title: Calibrate the judge and evaluate how the system selects a usable answer
points: Calibrate judges against independently reviewed cases; adjudicate disagreement.
Inspect serious false passes, false failures, and repeated-run variability.
pass@k asks whether at least one of k attempts meets the success test.
Production also needs a selection rule, acceptable single-run behavior, and full retry cost.

visualData.caption: Proposed judge-validation method; attempt example is synthetic

cells: FALSE FAILURE · inspect lost utility/review burden

visualData.attemptLesson: This one case can count as solved at k=3 under an at-least-one-success test. It does not show that the system can select attempt 2 or reliably succeed on the first attempt.
visualData.suggestedVisual: Two panels: a labeled 2×2 judge disagreement matrix without invented rates, and a three-attempt strip with one passing answer. Prominently label the strip synthetic.

readerNotes: Treat the judge as another evaluated system. Use independently reviewed examples, retain expert disagreement, and adjudicate important conflicts rather than treating one person's label as infallible. Check high-consequence false passes separately from overall agreement. A fail-leaning judge can also reject useful work and increase human burden; stricter grading is a hypothesis to test, not proof of reliability.

In standard pass@k evaluation, a task counts as solved when at least one of k sampled candidates meets the specified test, then results are summarized across tasks. It measures a multi-attempt success opportunity, not the reliability of the first answer or the deployed system's ability to choose a correct candidate. The primary HumanEval paper explicitly separates oracle-like selection from practical candidate selection. No numerical result from that paper or from a company is claimed here.

Provenance: Ramp's Day 2 notes mention pass@k without k, scoring rules, or results. The banking session records a fail-leaning configurable judge, with Comet/NatWest affiliation unresolved. Upstart's advertised abstract describes human calibration for voice-agent judges; it is agenda evidence, not an attendee observation. Its automated self-improvement loops are described as under development, not achieved self-healing.
speakerNotes: Spend the first half on the dangerous top-right cell: the judge passes an unacceptable output. Ask whether a system could have excellent average agreement while missing rare severe defects. Then acknowledge the opposite cost: a judge that fails everything is not useful.

Use the attempt strip to prevent a common metric misunderstanding. There is one successful candidate, but someone must recognize it. The end-to-end retry and selection policy must be evaluated and costed. The illustration is one synthetic case, not an empirical pass@3 estimate.
slides.lead: Reliable evaluation requires both a trustworthy grader and a tested candidate-selection policy. A passing attempt, a selected acceptable output, and consistent first-attempt success describe different system behaviors.

insights.title: Calibrate against reviewed cases
insights.text: Compare judge decisions with independently reviewed examples and adjudicate important disagreements. Inspect serious false passes separately from overall agreement. Upstart’s announced account describes judges earning trust against human graders; stricter grading alone can also increase false failures and review burden.

insights.title: Separate attempts from selection
insights.text: pass@k concerns at least one successful candidate among k attempts under a defined test. In the synthetic three-attempt strip, the second candidate passes. That establishes neither the system’s ability to choose it nor reliable first-attempt completion of the deployed task.

insights.title: Price the deployed retry policy
insights.text: Report the acceptance test, k, single-attempt results, selection success, and total retry cost together. Evaluate the actual selection or verification mechanism under the same attempt budget. Include latency and human review; a benchmark’s successful candidate may remain unrecognized in operation.

slides.evidenceNote: Judge matrix is a proposed method; the three-attempt strip is synthetic. Ramp and the banking account are unverified notes; Upstart is program context. The method paper supports the pass@k distinction.

slides.title: Hold the workload fixed while testing one system change at a time
points: Replay baseline and candidate on the same input snapshots and assessment cases.
Vary skills, memory, context, or model deliberately; inspect the paired failures.
Track task/evidence quality, critical defects, review effort, latency, and cost.
Retest fixes on known failures and a separate assessment set.

visualData.caption: Illustrative experiment plan · cells are measurements to collect, not company results
visualData.suggestedVisual: A compact comparison matrix with words rather than fabricated scores. Highlight one row at a time; below it show the variables held fixed.

readerNotes: Compare changes on matched cases so that task mix, source freshness, or grader changes do not masquerade as an improvement. Where feasible, vary one component at a time. For stochastic systems, use repeated assessments sufficient to examine uncertainty; compare distributions and important failure examples rather than only a single run's aggregate.

Ramp's Day 2 notes record experiments described as working: reducing an eight-skill bundle to four, trajectory-distilled memory, and shrinking an Excel skill. No effect sizes, controlled assessment details, or repeated-run results were captured. The method motivates an ablation design; the recorded counts are neither recommended defaults nor proof that reducing context always helps.

The proposed matrix adds explicit review and full attempt cost to the quality vector. Retest a discovered failure, but retain an assessment set not selected solely because it contains known failures. Otherwise an iteration can overfit the observed incidents while harming ordinary work. This is editorial methodology, not a claim that Ramp followed this exact protocol.
speakerNotes: The point is not to build this entire matrix before starting. Choose the next decision, hold the case set fixed, and compare one candidate against a working baseline. Show that even a seemingly obvious improvement—another skill, more memory—must earn its place.

Ask what would change our mind: better average scores with a new high-severity failure should trigger investigation, not an automatic win. Separate the cases used to fix a problem from those used to assess the final change.
slides.lead: Ablations make context, skills, memory, and model changes accountable to the complete job. Paired comparisons reveal improvements and regressions that disappear when task mix or grader behavior changes.

insights.title: Control the comparison conditions
insights.text: Replay baseline and candidate on matched tasks with the same source snapshots, permissions, rubric, evaluator version, and attempt policy. Change one component where feasible. Repeat stochastic assessments to inspect variation and paired failures; one aggregate run can conceal an unstable advantage.

insights.title: Use ablations to challenge intuition
insights.text: Ramp described reducing an eight-skill bundle to four, shrinking an Excel skill, and what it called trajectory-distilled memory: memory derived from prior agent runs. The notes do not capture its construction or measured effect. Test each component’s contribution instead of assuming that more memory or fewer skills always helps.

insights.title: Protect an independent assessment set
insights.text: Turn discovered failures into regression cases, while retaining a separate assessment set covering ordinary and difficult work. Compare evidence quality, critical defects, review effort, latency, and full cost. A fix earns its place only within explicitly agreed quality and operating tradeoffs.

slides.title: Release decisions need explicit blockers, accountable judgment, and bounded exposure
points: Predeclare blocking conditions and acceptable quality/operating tradeoffs.
Review critical failures, paired regressions, uncertainty, and evaluator validity.
Retain the cases, versions, traces, decisions, and approved exceptions.
Roll out in stages with explicit stop, rollback, and renewed-review conditions.

visualData.caption: Illustrative release logic · proposed framework, not a firm's approved policy

decisions.name: BLOCK / investigate
decisions.condition: A blocking condition fails, evidence is inadequate, or a material regression is unresolved.

decisions.name: PROMOTE within agreed scope
decisions.condition: Predeclared checks meet the decision's standard, accountable review accepts the evidence, and monitoring/rollback are ready.

visualData.caveat: No critical failure observed in a finite suite is not proof that critical failures cannot occur.
visualData.suggestedVisual: An evidence packet enters a gate with a separate red blocking lane and a blue quality/tradeoff lane. Both feed an accountable decision; monitoring follows release rather than disappearing after it.

readerNotes: Define the release decision's standard before seeing the candidate's results. Critical conditions may include unauthorized access, unsupported consequential claims, or missing required approval; which conditions block a release is a domain decision. Keep those conditions separate from graded usefulness. A finite assessment can support a bounded decision, but a clean test run is not a proof of zero risk.

Retain a reviewable evidence packet: intended use and scope, case/evaluator/system versions, results by important slice, material disagreement, representative traces, known limitations, exception decisions, and operational stop conditions. Repeat or broaden assessment when uncertainty could change the decision. Do not invent a universal pass threshold or regard a single combined accuracy score as sufficient.

The banking notes record multidimensional quality and a configurable fail-leaning judge, but no actual reviewer approval package, release threshold, or rollback trigger. Its current NatWest versus earlier Comet attribution remains unresolved. The gate shown here is an editorial proposal informed by that discussion and the Day 1 system-failure perspective; it is not attributed as an implemented bank policy.
speakerNotes: Return to the synthetic rubric: excellent arithmetic cannot compensate for an unauthorized send. The gate preserves that logic at release level. Ask the team to name a blocker and the evidence needed to test it, rather than choose a convenient overall percentage.

Emphasize bounded scope and accountable judgment. Tests inform a release decision; monitoring and rollback address what the suite did not foresee. We are not claiming that any speaker supplied this exact evidence packet.
slides.lead: A release gate combines critical conditions with useful-work evidence and an accountable decision. Passing a finite suite supports a scoped judgment; it cannot establish that consequential failures are impossible.

insights.title: Declare blockers before scoring
insights.text: Specify prohibited access or actions, unsupported consequential claims, and omitted approvals before reviewing candidate results. Keep these conditions outside a compensating average. The banking session’s quality-vector discussion motivates multidimensional review, but supplied no captured release threshold or implemented rollback policy.

insights.title: Assemble a reviewable evidence packet
insights.text: Retain intended scope, task and evaluator versions, results by important slice, representative traces, material regressions, expert disagreements, and known limits. Name the accountable decision owner and record accepted exceptions. Inadequate evidence is a reason to investigate before expanding exposure.

insights.title: Limit promotion and monitor outcomes
insights.text: Promote only within agreed scope, with operational monitoring and explicit pause, rollback, or renewed-review conditions. A clean finite assessment does not prove zero risk. Broaden or repeat testing when unresolved uncertainty could change the decision, and retain authority outside automated diagnosis.

slides.title: Convert production failures into reviewed tests before changing agent behavior
points: Observe complete traces and human corrections; triage by consequence.
Turn a failure into a versioned case and a proposed change.
Test the candidate against regressions and separate assessment cases.
Review, release in scope, monitor, and stop or roll back when conditions fail.

visualData.caption: Proposed controlled improvement loop · not a claim of autonomous self-healing

controlPoints.label: Distinguish model failure, missing evidence, tool/runtime failure, and evaluator error.
Keep the assessment set separate from the cases used to tune the change.
An automated diagnosis or proposed fix is not permission to deploy.
Capture drift, escaped defects, corrections, and full operating cost.

visualData.chapterExit: A first useful artifact: one task contract, a small case set, an explicit rubric, a baseline comparison, and an accountable release decision.
visualData.suggestedVisual: Seven-node loop with human/accountability markers at adjudication and release. Use a red branch from monitoring to pause/rollback; do not animate an automatic production-change arrow.

readerNotes: Connect monitoring to decisions and experiments, not merely dashboards. Capture enough context to reproduce important behavior: request, available sources and permissions, tool interactions, output, reviewer correction, relevant versions, and evaluation results. Authorized handling of traces and sensitive data remains a prerequisite; collecting more telemetry is not permission to expose private content.

Arize's Day 1 notes describe a build/evaluate/trace-inspection/improvement loop and agents consuming telemetry. The product and skill names were recorded uncertainly, and no diagnostic accuracy or autonomous remediation result was captured. The controlled loop shown here adds explicit adjudication, assessment separation, and release authority as editorial recommendations.

Upstart's advertised session describes moving from human call review toward human-calibrated judges, with automated self-improvement loops still being built. That is agenda-based, speaker-reported context rather than an attended-case result. Use it to ask what evidence permits reduced review; do not present it as proof that a self-healing production system was achieved.
speakerNotes: Close the chapter by tracing a failure around the loop. The failure becomes a test; a proposed change must prove it helps without causing an unacceptable regression. An agent can assist with diagnosis or propose a skill edit, while approval to change production remains explicit.

Give the team a manageable next step: one workflow, a small reviewable case set, a rubric, and a baseline. Add infrastructure when the working loop requires it. Invite discussion about which failure class deserves the first dedicated test.
slides.lead: A controlled improvement loop connects observations to reproducible cases, assessed changes, and authorized releases. Trace analysis can suggest a repair; evidence and accountable judgment determine whether that repair should operate.

insights.title: Capture enough context to reproduce
insights.text: Record the request, permitted sources and actions, tool interactions, output, human correction, and relevant versions. Triage whether the defect concerns evidence, reasoning, runtime behavior, or the evaluator itself. Handle traces under existing access rules; observability does not authorize exposing sensitive content.

insights.title: Turn diagnosis into an experiment
insights.text: Arize described using agent traces to identify issues and improvement opportunities. Reproduce a suspected failure, add a versioned case, and propose a specific change. Assess it against regressions and separate cases before accepting the diagnosis; automated suggestions are still hypotheses requiring verification.

insights.title: Keep release authority explicit
insights.text: Require accountable review before a proposed repair changes production behavior, then monitor escaped defects, corrections, drift, and full operating cost. Upstart’s announced self-improvement loops remained under development. Use these accounts to design a controlled process without assuming autonomous remediation has been demonstrated.

slides.title: Reusable skills must encode expert reasons, required questions, and limits
points: Pick a frequent workflow with judgeable results.
Teach the reasoning, required questions, and limits.

steps.label: Teach
steps.detail: Narrate why in a representative case

visualData.caption: Five steps captured in the notes; owner/reviewer and peer review are fresh agenda context.
visualData.evidenceLabel: Range confirmed by user; Matt Ragone / Range in refreshed October 14 official record.

readerNotes: The user confirmed that the financial-planner example was Range. The refreshed official schedule identifies Matt Ragone and “We Let Our Financial Planners Write the Agents.” The attendee notes capture the five-step skill-building method and human-reviewed drafting while a planner works with another client. The fresh abstract says planners write and maintain skills used daily and peer-review them like plans; this supports speaker-reported operational use, not independently verified outcomes.

Owner/reviewer requirements are fresh agenda context rather than a detail captured in the freeform notes. The abstract’s six-month/24-skill/17-planning-skill figures and five-to-ten-case testing example are not universal targets and are intentionally omitted from the visible method. Source identity must be versioned: this UUID referred to an NVIDIA reranker session in the October 10 snapshot and to Range in the October 14 snapshot.
speakerNotes: Emphasize the difference between general financial knowledge and how a firm performs a particular workflow. Domain experts can make required questions and limits explicit, while technical teams help make the behavior inspectable and testable.
A skill is a maintained work instruction with ownership. The five steps organize the work; they do not guarantee appropriate advice or safe deployment.
slides.lead: Range’s planners describe turning their own methods into agent skills. Pick–Teach–Pack–Test–Ship makes judgment explicit, while ownership and peer review keep the instructions maintainable as practice changes.

insights.title: Teach the firm’s method
insights.text: Range distinguishes general planning knowledge from how its professionals deliver recommendations. Start with a repeated workflow whose result an expert can judge, then narrate a representative case and the reasons behind decisions. Capture judgment rather than asking the agent to imitate a polished answer.

insights.title: Package questions and limits
insights.text: A skill needs required client inputs, ways to obtain authorized information, clarification questions, and boundaries it must respect. Missing facts should change the workflow, not invite invented assumptions. Make exceptions and handoff conditions explicit enough to test on difficult cases.

insights.title: Maintain an accountable instruction
insights.text: Range’s current abstract describes planners maintaining skills and peer-reviewing them like plans. Assign an owner and reviewer, retain change history, and retest revisions. Include incomplete facts and conflicting instructions to check when the skill clarifies, hands off or refuses an unsupported conclusion.

points: Gather only authorized inputs and surface missing data.
Produce an evidence-linked draft with checked calculations.

steps: Compute and assemble a review packet
Edit or reject; decide the next step

readerNotes: This fictional workflow illustrates the Range note’s parallel drafting and human review. The invented amounts show a simple calculation, not a real client, a real product outcome, or financial advice. No claim is made that Range uses these exact components or that the arithmetic difference supports a financial recommendation.

Wise’s agenda-only description separates model proposals from authority and describes versioned platform policies. The swimlane is our proposed design: data access, drafting, review, and execution are different responsibilities. Human review needs clear evidence and an enforceable boundary; merely labeling a person “in the loop” does not prove an effective control.
speakerNotes: Walk horizontally through the lanes. The agent prepares work while the professional retains judgment. An executor should not infer its authority from a fluent draft or a model’s confidence.
Invite the audience to name one missing input or one action that must remain blocked. Keep the example at the review-packet level; it is not advice.
slides.lead: The synthetic review packet separates authorized facts, agent preparation, professional judgment, and execution. Its USD 36,000 arithmetic difference supports inspection, not an affordability conclusion or a product recommendation.

insights.title: Separate facts from judgment
insights.text: The fictional inputs show annual income of USD 120,000 and recorded expenses of USD 84,000. Their USD 36,000 difference is arithmetic, not disposable capacity or an insurance need. The agent should expose missing facts and assumptions rather than infer suitability from this subtraction.

insights.title: Make review a decision
insights.text: Range’s vignette has an agent draft another client’s analysis while a planner serves someone else, followed by review and adjustment. A useful review packet exposes inputs, calculations, gaps, and proposed conclusions. Evaluate accepted work after corrections, rather than counting drafts as completed professional service.

insights.title: Keep execution authority separate
insights.text: Wise’s framework description separates model proposals from authority to act. In this proposed workflow, reviewing a draft does not automatically authorize sending it or executing a transaction. A separate service should enforce the permitted action and retain who approved it, for which case.

Apply policy independently of the model’s proposed action.

sideControls.label: Approval triage
sideControls.detail: Classifier output is a signal, not authority

visualData.caption: Proposed control pattern. Two Sigma notes describe components; Wise agenda describes reasoning/authority separation.
visualData.evidenceLabel: Two Sigma: attendee notes, production marked speaker-reported. Wise: agenda-only system/framework account.

readerNotes: The Two Sigma notes record an agent registry, risk-factor scoring, access declarations, active controls, common evaluations, and an independent classifier for approval triage. The attendee marked the talk production, but no coverage, calibrated classifier performance, or measured safety/utility result was captured. The classifier’s type and enforcement powers are unspecified; do not call it deterministic or assume it can safely waive approvals.

Wise’s official abstract describes LOOP and versioned policies separating reasoning from authority. It is agenda-only evidence in this presentation. The diagram is a proposed synthesis, not a disclosed complete architecture from either firm. Evaluate denied requests, revocation, retries, cross-user scope, and exceptions before treating a valid tool call as an appropriate business action.
speakerNotes: Show the authority path as clearly as the data path. A model can suggest a tool call, while a different component decides whether it may execute under the user’s scope and the task’s rules.
Ask which checks are enforced outside the model and what happens when a classifier is wrong. An approval workflow needs measurable false-pass and false-alarm behavior as well as clear ownership.
slides.lead: Two Sigma describes ownership, declared access, risk scoring, and active controls; Wise separates reasoning from authority. Together, these ideas make the permission path as explicit as the data path.

insights.title: Make agents owned systems
insights.text: Two Sigma’s registry records owners, products, tools, and evaluations, with risk scoring informed by access and controls. Use that inventory to locate responsibility and identify required checks. Registration provides visibility; it is not evidence that an agent’s permissions or behavior are constrained.

insights.title: Enforce the requested scope
insights.text: A model can propose a tool call while policy decides whether the user, case, resource, and action are permitted. Test revoked access, cross-user scope, retries, and duplicate requests. A valid credential or technically successful API call does not establish an appropriate business action.

insights.title: Treat triage as fallible
insights.text: The Two Sigma notes mention an independent classifier for deciding when human approval is needed, without performance or enforcement details. Evaluate missed consequential cases and unnecessary interruptions. A classifier’s output can inform review routing; its independence alone does not justify waiving required approval.

loops.detail: Inspect generated work and catch local issues

loops.label: Release loop

readerNotes: The Sonar notes record a conceptual “code confidence” product of intent, guardrails, verification, and evidence, along with warnings about human over-reliance, codebase complexity, compounding errors, and inconsistent model judges. Treat the four factors as a design checklist rather than a calibrated score or probability. No scale, formula validation, or defect-rate prediction was captured.

The three loops are from the official abstract, not explicitly recorded in the notes. They suggest different places to check generated work, pre-release behavior, and production repairs. The recorded 50k-line example has no benchmark setup and is not a universal limit. Neither the notes nor abstract establishes automated prevention of all defects or a proven customer deployment.
speakerNotes: Connect the loops to the failure they can catch. A local generator check may miss a system invariant; CI may miss a rare runtime interaction; maintenance needs to verify that a repair did not create a new regression.
Keep “prevention first” as a priority, not a claim that later detection and response are unnecessary. Independent verification remains work to design and validate.
slides.lead: Sonar’s three-loop framing places checks during generation, before release, and after deployment. Intent, guardrails, verification, and evidence form a design checklist—not a calibrated confidence formula.

insights.title: Prevent local mistakes early
insights.text: The creation loop guides generated work with explicit goals, standards, and constraints, then checks local changes before they accumulate. It can reduce avoidable rework in principle, but needs evaluation. Agreement from another model or a quick human approval is not independent correctness evidence.

insights.title: Verify the system before release
insights.text: Release checks should examine behavior beyond the edited fragment: interfaces, permissions, financial invariants, and regressions. Keep reproducible test evidence and assess whether the checker detects important defects. Neither a passing suite nor a fail-leaning judge establishes that every consequential failure has been covered.

insights.title: Verify repairs during operation
insights.text: Production observations reveal failures the pre-release assessment missed. Turn an incident into a reproducible case, test the repair alongside other workloads, and retain rollback conditions. Prevention remains a priority, while detection and response remain necessary; the framework does not establish autonomous self-healing.

Keep state, retries, and idempotency under system control.

readerNotes: Vanguard’s official abstract describes a production cash-ledger modernization with separate producer migration, gold-copy replication, and consumer migration; CDC synchronization, GraphQL decoupling, and database-layer idempotency are highlighted. AI tooling is described as helping maintain two codebases. This is agenda-only context: no attended-note block for Vanguard was supplied.

The transferable point is that faster engineering does not remove financial consistency responsibilities. The abstract does not isolate AI’s contribution, publish productivity or risk improvements, or describe an autonomous investor/adviser agent. The simplified map is a description of the advertised case, not a recommendation to introduce dual systems or a compatibility layer into another product.
speakerNotes: Use this case to bring the chapter back to system engineering. An agent can accelerate a code change, but the financial process still needs complete transactions, consistent state, and safe repeat execution.
When reporting a large project’s outcome, separate the architecture that preserved correctness from the incremental benefit attributed to AI. Neither should be assumed from the other.
slides.lead: Vanguard’s ledger-modernization account separates producer migration, replicated financial state, and consumer migration. AI-assisted engineering remains subordinate to transaction completeness, consistency, controlled retries, and reviewable reconciliation.

insights.title: Map the financial dependencies
insights.text: Vanguard describes independently progressing producer and consumer migrations around a replicated gold copy, with change data capture (CDC) synchronization and decoupled access. The useful lesson is to identify where financial state originates, changes, and is consumed. This case structure is not a prescription for every modernization.

insights.title: Make invariants directly observable
insights.text: Database-layer idempotency is highlighted in Vanguard’s account. Translate completeness, duplicate prevention, and consistency into observable checks at the relevant boundaries, including retry and recovery paths. Faster code generation cannot demonstrate that no transaction was omitted or that a repeated operation is safe.

insights.title: Isolate the contribution of AI
insights.text: Vanguard says AI tools helped maintain two codebases, without isolating their incremental benefit. Separate the migration controls that preserved financial behavior from any improvement in engineering effort. Compare equivalent changes, review and rework, correctness, and operating cost before attributing the whole project’s outcome to AI.

slides.title: An AI engineer owns the loop from user need to verified improvement
points: Translate a need into task success.
Instrument behavior and diagnose failures.
Verify fixes before changing the workflow.
Retain an accountable release decision.

visualData.case: Arize attendee notes: build/evaluate/read traces/identify improvements; Ramp: assess whole-task changes
visualData.caption: Editorial operating loop derived from recorded mechanisms; not a verified autonomous-remediation system.

readerNotes: Arize's recorded distinction is between working on a feature and building the system that repeatedly improves it. Ramp's notes add a task-level definition of success and experiments on skills and memory. Together they suggest an engineer's growth path centered on closing a reliable loop from user need to evidence-backed change.

Evidence: Arize is a vendor account with unclear maturity and no measured diagnostic results in the notes. Ramp's notes omit an explicit evidence/maturity label. Automated diagnosis should remain a hypothesis until a concrete issue is reproduced and a change is tested; named tools or skills from rough notes are not required to apply this operating principle.
speakerNotes: Connect this chapter to the preceding reliability material: engineering responsibility continues after the first successful demonstration. Read traces to understand failures, then make a change whose effect can be checked.
Keep diagnosis, proposing a fix, validation and release authority separate. This is a useful skill model even when each step is performed manually.
slides.lead: Professional growth comes from connecting task definition, instrumentation, evaluation, diagnosis and release. A working feature becomes a dependable capability through repeated, reviewable decisions about what to change and why.

insights.title: Instrument the complete task
insights.text: Arize described using traces to identify issues and improvement opportunities. Capture the request, source context, intermediate actions, result, evaluation and relevant versions together. A useful trace lets an engineer reconstruct why a workflow failed, rather than merely observing that it did.

insights.title: Build a portfolio of decisions
insights.text: Maintain a small portfolio of reproducible failures, baseline comparisons, repairs and release decisions. For each entry, explain the domain problem, system behavior, evidence and tradeoff. This makes growth observable through stronger engineering judgment, rather than through a longer list of tools.

insights.title: Close the release loop
insights.text: Keep issue discovery, proposed fixes, validation and permission to release as separate responsibilities. Preserve the test evidence and decision, then observe the changed workflow for regressions. The conference mechanisms motivate this operating habit; they do not establish autonomous remediation or validated diagnostic accuracy.

slides.title: Technical fluency must connect domain meaning, system behavior and measurement
points: Domain: define the decision and its limits.
Data: preserve meaning, access and provenance.
Systems: make state and authority explicit.
Measurement: validate tasks, judges and value.
Communication: show the evidence and uncertainty.

cards.practice: Turn a professional's judgment into inputs, questions and acceptance criteria
Inspect entity, time, units, source and transformations
Draw ownership, allowed actions, state and exceptions
Separate critical failures, task success, judge errors and full cost
Explain what was claimed, observed, checked and still unknown

visualData.caption: Proposed competency map for this audience; no measured industry skill ranking.

readerNotes: The recurring engineering responsibilities span domain understanding, data semantics, software controls, measurement and communication. A data scientist can contribute experimental design and uncertainty analysis; an engineer can make behavior observable and enforceable; a technical lead can align the workflow and decision criteria. These responsibilities overlap and can be learned through shared work.

This is an editorial growth framework derived from the conference mechanisms, not a survey of hiring requirements or a claim that any firm uses this competency model. Choose a development area by inspecting a real gap in a bounded workflow, rather than collecting tools without a task.
speakerNotes: Invite the audience to identify one responsibility it already performs well and one that would most improve its current work. The goal is balanced fluency and good collaboration, not requiring every person to become the sole expert in every area.
Keep evidence communication in the map. Being able to distinguish a useful mechanism from an unsupported outcome is part of technical judgment.
slides.lead: Develop the responsibilities together on a real workflow. Domain expertise defines acceptable work; data and software make it reproducible; evaluation and communication determine which claims the evidence can support.

insights.title: Translate judgment into inputs
insights.text: Use Range's procedural example to ask a domain expert which facts matter, why a step is necessary and when clarification is required. Connect that reasoning to entities, periods, units and source definitions so an agent can access the right information.

insights.title: Connect controls to tests
insights.text: Draw who requests work, which resources are available, what may execute and how exceptions are handled. Then design cases that challenge those boundaries and the evaluator itself. System design and experimental design should meet at observable behavior, including serious false passes.

insights.title: Communicate a defensible decision
insights.text: Explain the task, mechanism, comparison, result and remaining uncertainty in one evidence card. Distinguish a reported deployment from tested effectiveness and a useful output from attributable business value. This practice helps data scientists, engineers and technical leads review the same decision.

slides.title: Software lifespan changes maintenance needs; failure consequences still determine required checks
points: Expected lifespan shapes maintenance investment.
Dependencies can turn an experiment into infrastructure.
Sensitive data and consequential actions still need checks.

cells.label: Simple and removable
cells.detail: Clear scope, owner and retirement condition

cells.label: Constrained and checked
cells.detail: Bounded execution and evidence before use

cells.label: Operated and verified
cells.detail: Explicit controls, recovery and continuing validation

visualData.caption: Editorial decision aid. The matrix is not Capital One policy or an assurance score.

readerNotes: Capital One's recorded discussion distinguishes durable software from software that might be replaced in hours and used by relatively few people. A practical interpretation is to allocate maintainability deliberately. Expected lifespan is only one axis: a short-lived tool can still expose sensitive data or produce a consequential financial error.

Evidence: the Capital One notes are conceptual and do not establish a deployed disposable-software model or near-zero replacement cost. Sonar and Two Sigma supply complementary prevention/control concerns. The matrix is a proposed engineering judgment aid; specific checks depend on the actual workflow and existing requirements.
speakerNotes: Use the short-lived/high-consequence quadrant to surface the tension. Cheap regeneration changes the economics of maintenance, but it does not make the consequences of a wrong answer disappear.
Ask what happens when a useful experiment gains downstream users. Reassess ownership, dependencies and validation instead of continuing to call it disposable.
slides.lead: Capital One's durability discussion separates short-lived tools from long-lived dependencies. Use lifespan and consequence as independent design questions, then revisit both when an experiment gains users or responsibilities.

insights.title: Allocate maintenance deliberately
insights.text: Capital One contrasted durable software with tools replaceable in hours and used by relatively few people. That framing can guide documentation, interfaces and maintenance investment. The notes do not demonstrate zero replacement cost or a deployed disposable-software model at the firm.

insights.title: Protect immediate business consequences
insights.text: A short-lived tool can still expose sensitive information, calculate a wrong financial figure or trigger an inappropriate action. Keep the relevant access, numerical and execution checks even when implementation is simple. Cheap regeneration does not reduce the consequence of an incorrect result.

insights.title: Reassess growing dependencies early
insights.text: When other people or workflows begin relying on an experiment, reassess ownership, support, recovery and regression coverage. Set a retirement condition for genuinely temporary tools. Continued use should trigger an explicit maintenance decision rather than quietly converting an experiment into infrastructure.

slides.title: One bounded experiment can develop the full engineering discipline
points: Choose one work product and a credible baseline.
Build the smallest complete path.
Inspect failures and change one variable.
Write the decision to continue, revise or retire.

stages.deliverable: Working path + traces + failure cases + comparison

visualData.caption: Optional learning exercise; no Fidelity project, owner, deadline or resource commitment is assumed.

readerNotes: A bounded experiment can develop the five responsibilities together. Start from a task a domain reviewer understands, use approved or synthetic material, and establish what accepted completion means. Instrument the complete path before expanding it. Keep assessment examples distinct from tuning, and evaluate severe failures separately from average quality.

This is a proposed learning exercise grounded in Ramp's task/ablation account, Arize's improvement-loop account and Contour's comparison questions. It is not a production approval process, sufficient statistical validation or a commitment for any existing project. Agree criteria before interpreting a result and preserve uncertainty when the sample is small.
speakerNotes: Make the exercise feel achievable: the deliverable is a defensible comparison and a decision, not an elaborate platform. A useful outcome can be that a deterministic workflow solves the task more simply, or that the data is not ready.
End the growth chapter by emphasizing the habit of making each claim reviewable. That habit transfers across models and tools.
slides.lead: Choose a work product a reviewer understands and build the smallest complete path. Learn by comparing behavior, inspecting failures and explaining a decision to continue, revise or retire.

insights.title: Frame a measurable task
insights.text: Select a research brief, analytical query result or preparation draft with clear users and acceptance criteria. Use approved or synthetic inputs and record current quality, time and effort. A useful learning exercise starts with the baseline, not the preferred model.

insights.title: Change one variable deliberately
insights.text: Follow Ramp's experimental direction by varying a skill bundle, memory rule or model while holding assessment cases and input snapshots fixed. Include ordinary, ambiguous and consequential-failure cases. Measure accepted quality, review effort, latency and cost together; keep tuning separate from assessment.

insights.title: Finish with an evidence card
insights.text: Document the comparison, observed failures, uncertainty and next decision. A valid outcome may be a simpler deterministic workflow, inadequate data or an experiment worth stopping. Share one reproducible case with a peer and explain what evidence would change your conclusion.

slides.title: Turn the conference into three decisions and one bounded comparison
points: Choose the valuable work product.
Define evidence and authority boundaries.
Agree quality, review-cost and value criteria.
Propose one bounded comparison.

decisions.name: Boundary
decisions.prompt: Which sources, actions and human judgments are permitted?

decisions.name: Evidence

readerNotes: The conference's useful return is a set of decisions peers can assess. Across the recorded examples, the recurring responsibilities are task-specific information, procedural knowledge, constrained action, independent checks, calibrated evaluation and value comparison. Those ideas become useful when attached to a narrow work product and a testable hypothesis.

A useful report-back separates mechanisms we can apply from effects we still need to measure. Keep company attributions and disclosure dates with the evidence, then define the local comparison needed to support a stronger claim about quality, capacity or business impact.
speakerNotes: Return to the opening work-product question. Ask the audience to propose a workflow, then fill the boundary and evidence columns before debating tools.
Leave ownership and dates as decisions for the team. The presentation proposes a way to decide; it does not announce a Fidelity commitment.
slides.lead: The useful return is a decision peers can assess: which work matters, which boundaries must hold and which evidence would justify change. Attach those decisions to one testable hypothesis.

insights.title: Choose the accepted work
insights.text: Name the person whose work should improve and the output they can inspect, correct and accept. Use the financial examples to sharpen that choice: a research insight, reviewed planning analysis or evidence-backed artifact. State the bottleneck before choosing tools or architecture.

insights.title: Define evidence and authority
insights.text: Specify the permitted sources, information cutoff, calculations, actions and human judgments. Identify what must remain blocked and what happens when evidence is missing. Bridgewater, Kepler and Two Sigma offer mechanisms to examine; the appropriate boundary depends on the particular workflow.

insights.title: Agree the comparison first
insights.text: Compare the candidate with the existing process on equivalent work, agreed acceptance criteria and critical conditions. Include all attempts and human effort. Decide beforehand which evidence would support continuing, repairing or retiring the approach; conference claims alone do not establish internal readiness.
