slides.title: Use disagreement to choose the next test
points: Which workflow has a consequential bottleneck?
Which failure could survive current review?
What baseline would change our mind?

cards.label: Value
cards.prompt: Name one accepted work product and the person whose work improves.

cards.label: Risk
cards.prompt: Name one unsupported fact, denied action or missed exception that matters.

cards.label: Test
cards.prompt: Name the comparison and evidence needed to continue, revise or stop.

visualData.closingLine: Choose a useful workflow. Preserve the evidence. Test the whole system.
visualData.caption: Discussion follows the 40-minute presentation; prompts do not imply any existing system deficiency.

readerNotes: Use these prompts to connect the industry examples to the audience's judgment without presuming a specific current project. A useful discussion produces a clear work unit, a consequential failure to test and a credible comparison. Record unresolved questions and who could clarify them, rather than forcing consensus from incomplete conference evidence.

The risk prompt follows the recorded failure-driven evaluation principle; the baseline prompt follows Contour's value-attribution discussion. Both are proposed uses of speaker accounts, not validated assurance methods or an endorsement of a particular tool.
speakerNotes: Introduce the three prompts in thirty seconds, then use the separately allocated discussion time. Start with silent individual thought or a concrete example so the conversation does not become a general tool debate.
Capture one candidate experiment and one unresolved evidence question. If no candidate meets the conditions, that is a useful outcome; no immediate project commitment is required.
slides.lead: End with a concrete workflow and a consequential uncertainty. Discussion should reveal the failure or comparison that could change the decision, rather than produce agreement around a favored tool.

insights.title: Expose the value assumption
insights.text: Ask which bottleneck limits the professional's work and what observable output would improve if it were removed. Challenge whether faster generation actually saves total effort after review. Record a measurable hypothesis instead of equating adoption, parallel drafting or user enthusiasm with value.

insights.title: Name the surviving failure
insights.text: Choose one unsupported fact, wrong period, denied action or missed exception that could pass ordinary review. Explain its consequence and where prevention, detection or intervention should operate. Use that case to test the complete workflow and the reviewer or judge.

insights.title: Capture the decision-changing evidence
insights.text: Agree what baseline, output checks, cost records or follow-up clarification would change the team's view. Leave ownership and timing for explicit discussion. If the evidence cannot yet support an experiment, record the missing prerequisite rather than forcing an immediate project commitment.

slides.title: One implementation checklist connects the task, evidence, authority and release decision
readerNotes: The checklist connects five responsibilities that are often assessed separately: task acceptance, evidence quality, action authority, evaluation and operation. Review them as one workflow so a correct-looking artifact cannot conceal a wrong source, unauthorized step or unreproducible release decision.

Use the contract to make disagreements concrete. A domain expert defines acceptable completion; data and engineering owners identify source semantics and enforceable boundaries; reviewers agree which failures block acceptance and what evidence permits a scoped change.

The checklist is an illustrative synthesis of the conference mechanisms. The source catalog preserves company attribution and historical dates; it does not turn a design pattern into independently verified business effectiveness.
speakerNotes: Use this reference page for a follow-up question or later study; it is outside the timed 40-minute path.
slides.lead: Use a shared contract before building and at each material change. It gives domain experts, data scientists and engineers a common way to review what the system should accomplish.

insights.title: Make each requirement testable
insights.text: Replace broad goals such as accuracy or safety with observable behavior. Name the work product, necessary evidence, allowed actions and unacceptable outcomes. A requirement is useful when a reviewer can recognize compliance and a test can expose a meaningful violation.

insights.title: Retain the decision context
insights.text: Record system, data, skill, case and evaluator versions together with the result. Keep important disagreement and accepted limitations. That record lets another person reproduce the comparison and understand why a change was considered appropriate for a particular scope.

insights.title: Revisit changes in exposure
insights.text: A new data source, user population, tool or execution permission can change the failure modes even if the prompt is unchanged. Reassess the relevant cases and operational controls. Expand review when the uncertainty could alter the decision, rather than repeating every check mechanically.

readerNotes: The atlas preserves all 25 firm perspectives from the consolidated industry research, including cases with sparse October 10 abstracts. These are selected, uneven, self-reported examples, not an industry survey or a ranking of frontier maturity.

insights.title: Compare like work with like
insights.text: A research information feed, planner preparation draft and code-migration assistant have different acceptance decisions. Compare systems performing equivalent work before interpreting adoption, time or cost. Their shared lesson is explicit evidence and control, not one universal success metric.

insights.title: Distinguish mechanism from effectiveness
insights.text: A detailed architecture explains how a system is intended to operate. Production use shows operational adoption. Neither alone establishes quality, net time saved or causal business impact. Ask what baseline, task mix and human effort would support the stronger claim.

insights.title: Use the atlas for follow-up
insights.text: The full reading-mode atlas retains 25 firm perspectives, source links and case limits. Use it to find a relevant peer pattern, then investigate the missing implementation detail or measurement. A company affiliation alone does not establish deployment of every discussed technique.

readerNotes: This is an illustrative schema for discussion, not a runnable framework. The purpose is to make the task, input snapshot, acceptance criteria, critical failures, case coverage, evaluator configuration, and release decision explicit.

The schema should be adapted to the particular decision. Choosing a model, reducing human review, and expanding action authority require different evidence. A finite assessment suite provides bounded evidence, not proof of absence of failure.

slides.lead: The illustrative schema links the intended task to inputs, case coverage, acceptance, critical conditions and an accountable owner. It is a compact specification to discuss before running an assessment.

insights.title: Define the permitted completion
insights.text: Describe the complete job, authorized data snapshot, output and action limits. Include when the system should clarify or abstain. Critical conditions need explicit definitions: unauthorized access is a failure; correctly refusing access can be the expected successful behavior.

insights.title: Version the evaluator as well
insights.text: A judge model, prompt, rubric or threshold change can change reported quality without changing the agent. Retain those versions with the case and system configuration. Recalibrate important decisions against reviewed examples when the evaluator changes or the task population shifts.

insights.title: Tie evidence to the decision
insights.text: Select cases and uncertainty analysis for the question being decided. Choosing a model, reducing review and granting execution authority require different evidence. The contract supports a scoped judgment with known limits; it cannot prove that no consequential failure remains possible.

A verified number can still be used in a wrong comparison. Preserve entity, metric definition, period, units/currency, source version, available-as-of time, and the calculation inputs and operations. The AsterCo values and documents are invented.

slides.lead: The synthetic AsterCo contract represents a 20% annual revenue-growth claim as a ratio. Its inputs, units, period, information cutoff and calculation are preserved for inspection and downstream rendering.

insights.title: Do not mix measurement types
insights.text: Revenue of 120 million dollars and revenue growth of 0.20 are different metrics with different units. Carry the metric definition and unit through every transformation. An exact numerical match against a document is insufficient if the answer uses the value in the wrong comparison.

insights.title: Retain the source identity
insights.text: Store the source document, passage, version and available-as-of time with each input. Reconstruct which evidence was eligible when the question was asked. Publication, reporting period and access permission answer different questions and should not be collapsed into a single timestamp.

insights.title: Propagate corrections through artifacts
insights.text: When an input is superseded, recompute dependent figures and update the associated narrative, table and chart. Preserve the earlier value and change reason for reproducibility. Validate the final artifact, since formatting or export can drop units, periods or links even when the calculation was correct.

slides.title: pass@k measures an opportunity to succeed; deployed reliability also requires choosing correctly
readerNotes: The primary HumanEval paper defines pass@k as an at-least-one-success benchmark across sampled candidates under a specified test and discusses candidate selection. This presentation borrows the metric distinction, not a code-benchmark performance result for finance.

A deployed workflow must identify and accept a usable answer, comply with critical conditions, and account for the costs of all attempts, verification, and review. Partial-credit task quality, pass@k, first-attempt success, and selected-output reliability should not be used interchangeably.
speakerNotes: Use this reference page for a follow-up question or later study; it is outside the timed 40-minute path.
slides.lead: Separate candidate generation from selection and acceptance. A multi-attempt benchmark can contain a passing answer while the deployed workflow selects a failing answer or spends excessive effort identifying the usable one.

insights.title: State the benchmark question
insights.text: Under pass@k, a task succeeds when at least one of k sampled candidates meets the specified test; results are summarized over tasks. State the task distribution, test and attempt budget. This does not report whether the first candidate succeeds or an operational selector finds the passing candidate.

insights.title: Evaluate the actual selector
insights.text: Run the verification, ranking or human-review process the deployed system will use. Measure acceptance of its chosen output, missed defects and rejection of usable candidates. Avoid interpreting an oracle-like benchmark that recognizes success using ground truth as a deployed selection capability.

insights.title: Count the entire attempt budget
insights.text: Include all generated candidates, tool calls, verification, review time and latency. Compare policies at explicit budgets and acceptance standards. More attempts can create an opportunity for higher success while increasing cost and exposure; evaluate that tradeoff on the actual workflow.

slides.title: Accepted-task rate and full cost reveal what adoption metrics leave unresolved
readerNotes: These are proposed measurement definitions. Define the population and exclusions in advance, record full workflow costs, and compare equivalent work at an agreed quality.

Contour’s notes call the approach A/B testing and describe a three-month tracking window, but assignment, sample size, controls, and causal estimates were not captured. Do not treat that window as sufficient validation for every financial workflow.
speakerNotes: Use this reference page for a follow-up question or later study; it is outside the timed 40-minute path.
slides.lead: Agree the eligible population, completion standard and comparison before reporting improvement. Pair output quality with operating effort so a reduction in one cost does not conceal increased work elsewhere.

insights.title: Use two complementary denominators
insights.text: Accepted-task rate uses all eligible assigned tasks to show how often the workflow succeeds. Cost per accepted task divides total workflow cost, including failed attempts, by accepted tasks. Report both; a low unit cost can coexist with too many unsuccessful or excluded tasks.

insights.title: Measure professional effort end-to-end
insights.text: Count preparation, correction, evidence checking, approval and follow-up, alongside system costs. Compare equivalent work at the same quality standard. Draft generation time alone cannot establish additional advisor or analyst capacity when people must reconstruct or repair the result.

insights.title: Separate process from business impact
insights.text: Faster accepted work is a process result. Attributable returns, client outcomes or revenue require an additional credible comparison and attention to selection and other drivers. Contour’s recorded comparison motivates the question; the notes do not establish a causal financial estimate.

slides.title: Turn unresolved conference claims into specific engineering follow-up questions
readerNotes: The source notes preserve unresolved terms such as “crunchable” and “roundedness”; these have not been silently corrected into a provider or safety metric. The Bridgewater reactive/proactive wording reverses once. Workbench examples suggest proactive attention guidance, but the terminology remains to verify.

Sonar’s roughly50k-line codebase example lacks model, workload, metric, and benchmark conditions. Its confidence multiplication is a conceptual framing. Kepler’s retrieval settings are incompletely captured. None is a universal engineering threshold or a calibrated assurance formula.

The failure study’s recorded expected-loss product has undefined events, conditional relationships, and severity units. Incident rankings and exponential growth claims lack denominators and methods in the notes. These are follow-up topics, not established prevalence or expected-loss estimates.
speakerNotes: Use this reference page for a follow-up question or later study; it is outside the timed 40-minute path.
slides.lead: Uncertainty becomes useful when it identifies the next inspection or test. Focus follow-up on coverage, failure handling, measurement and deployment scope rather than repeating an attractive claim without its conditions.

insights.title: Ask what the checker misses
insights.text: For citation verification, judge calibration or approval triage, ask which cases are assessed, which serious errors pass, and what happens when support fails. Independent components can share blind spots. Request representative failures and adjudication procedures alongside aggregate agreement or architecture diagrams.

insights.title: Ask what the result measures
insights.text: For reported time savings, productivity or financial effects, request the baseline, task population, exclusions, sample, uncertainty and full human effort. Clarify whether the figure describes adoption, a pilot, estimated opportunity or realized outcome. Preserve historical disclosure dates when comparing firms.

insights.title: Ask what scope was demonstrated
insights.text: Clarify production scope, user entitlements, model and data versions, and operational stop conditions. Sonar’s code-size example and Kepler’s rough retrieval settings lack enough context to become defaults. Unresolved note terms and the Comet/NatWest affiliation discrepancy remain in the source context for follow-up.
